package_info.why_malicious: These packages are brandjacking and typosquatting attacks that impersonate legitimate Maven and Jenkins plugins. Each contains backdoored code that downloads and executes arbitrary code from attacker-controlled C2 servers, enabling remote code execution, system compromise, and persistent access. The malicious payloads are triggered during normal plugin operations, targeting both developer machines and CI/CD build servers, and can propagate supply chain attacks.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (plugin execution during Maven build process)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During Maven build execution, this code downloads a remote JAR file from a hardcoded C2 server (http://swmail.malware.index/evilmaven.jar), dynamically loads it into the JVM using reflection, and executes a class from the downloaded JAR, enabling arbitrary code execution under the build process context.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code uses reflection to bypass normal classloader restrictions and loads code from an untrusted, hardcoded external URL, which is a classic remote code execution backdoor technique. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on any system running the plugin.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate Maven compiler plugin should never download or execute code from the internet during build execution. All dependencies should be resolved through trusted Maven repositories, not arbitrary URLs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic plugin loading is only legitimate when performed from trusted, signed repositories and with explicit user consent. Loading code from arbitrary URLs is never acceptable in production plugins.
key_indicators: Reflection to invoke addURL on URLClassLoader
Dynamic class loading (Class.forName) from downloaded JAR
No user interaction or consent required
Execution occurs during normal Maven build process

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On mail notification events in Jenkins, this code downloads a Groovy script from a hardcoded C2 server (http://112.11.168.47/evil.groovy), writes it to /tmp/evil.groovy, and immediately evaluates it using GroovyShell, executing arbitrary attacker-supplied code on the Jenkins server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and executing code from an untrusted remote server is a direct code execution backdoor. The use of GroovyShell to evaluate attacker-controlled scripts enables full remote code execution on the Jenkins server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A mail notification plugin should only handle email notifications and never download or execute remote scripts. Executing arbitrary code in response to notification events is a severe violation of expected plugin behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated script updates from trusted, signed sources are extremely rare and never appropriate for notification plugins. GroovyShell evaluation should only be used for trusted, static scripts.
key_indicators: Execution triggered by mail notification event
No validation or signature checking of downloaded script

execution_context.trigger: runtime (HTTP GET request to web application)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On every HTTP GET request, this servlet decodes a base64-encoded string to obtain a bash reverse shell command, then executes it, causing the server to connect back to the attacker's IP (45.87.122.54:8888) and provide remote shell access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code executes a base64-decoded reverse shell command on every HTTP GET request, providing the attacker with persistent remote shell access. This is a severe and overt backdoor.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A servlet API should never execute shell commands or open network connections to untrusted hosts. Servlets are expected to handle HTTP requests, not spawn shells or connect to external IPs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for reverse shell execution in servlet APIs. Process execution in servlets is extremely rare and should be tightly controlled and audited.
key_indicators: Use of Runtime.getRuntime().exec to spawn shell
Executes on every HTTP GET request

attack_chain.action: User or build system installs and executes the malicious plugin/component, mistaking it for a legitimate one due to brandjacking or typosquatting.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is triggered during normal plugin/component operation, such as build execution, mail notification, or HTTP request handling.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code downloads and executes attacker-controlled payloads or opens a reverse shell, enabling remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution or shell access for the attacker on the compromised system.

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains persistent access, can exfiltrate data, run arbitrary commands, or pivot to further attacks within the environment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise, potential for supply chain attack propagation to downstream users or systems.

behavioral_signatures: Plugins or components downloading and executing code from hardcoded external URLs during build or runtime
Use of reflection to dynamically load JARs from untrusted sources
GroovyShell evaluation of scripts fetched from remote servers
Base64-decoded shell commands executed at runtime within servlet or plugin code
Reverse shell connections initiated by Java processes in response to HTTP requests or plugin events
file_indicators: Presence of /tmp/evil.groovy on Jenkins or build servers
Unexpected modifications or additions to plugin JARs (CompilerMojo.class, MailWatcherNotification.class, HttpServlet.class)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for plugins or components that initiate outbound network requests to untrusted domains or IPs, especially during build, plugin execution, or HTTP request handling. Flag any use of reflection-based dynamic class loading, GroovyShell evaluation of remote scripts, or base64-decoded shell execution in plugin/component code. Alert on the presence of suspicious files such as /tmp/evil.groovy and on reverse shell connections initiated by Java processes. Use hash-based detection for known malicious JARs and monitor for unexpected changes to plugin classes.
